https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: People take part in a demonstration in defense of the international criminal court at Piazza Ugo La Malfa in Rome, Italy, on 16 July 2026. Photograph: Simona Granati/Corbis/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People take part in a demonstration in defense of the international criminal court at Piazza Ugo La Malfa in Rome, Italy, on 16 July 2026. Photograph: Simona Granati/Corbis/Getty Images Trump administration Human rights groups sue Trump administration over ‘crippling’ ICC sanctions Lawsuit challenges executive order targeting international criminal court for investigating Israeli crimes in Palestine Alice Speri Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.10 EDT First published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 10.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Four prominent US human rights organizations have accused the Trump administration of using its “crippling” sanctions regime against the international criminal court (ICC) to undermine global efforts to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity. In a lawsuit filed in federal court on Tuesday, the groups – the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch and the Open Society Institute – argued that the administration’s targeting of the ICC, as well as of groups and individuals affiliated with it or assisting its work, amounts to a “blatantly illegal attack on international justice”, the groups said. The suit challenges Trump’s February 2025 executive order , which authorized sanctions on ICC officials, judges and others working to support its investigation of Israeli crimes in Palestine – one of 18 investigations into war crimes and crimes against humanity the Netherlands-based tribunal is overseeing. US groups sue Trump administration claiming ICC sanctions violate first amendment Read more The US state department and justice department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The US government has long opposed and sought to impede the work of the court – of which it is not a party – but those attacks escalated after the ICC prosecutor issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant over crimes committed in Gaza. The US responded by sanctioning ICC prosecutors, judges, three leading Palestinian human rights groups and Francesca Albanese , the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Palestinian territory. Earlier this summer, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, also escalated efforts against the ICC, announcing a campaign aimed at “ dismantling ” it by pressuring member states to leave the court. Those attacks, and Trump’s executive order, undermine access to justice for victims of major human rights violations and criminalize the work of those seeking to combat impunity by collaborating with the court – including the plaintiffs in the case – in violation of both constitutional protections for free speech and association and US obligations under international law, the lawsuit argues. “The Trump administration took the extraordinary step to not only deny Palestinians and victims of US torture equal access to justice, but to criminalize and punish them, their lawyers and advocates, and their partners,” said Katherine Gallagher, a senior attorney at the Center for Constitutional Rights who represents victims before the ICC. “All victims of international crimes – from Sudan and Ukraine to Palestine and Afghanistan – need and deserve to have an independent and strong ICC able to fulfill its mission of ending impunity, without fear or favor.” The individuals placed under US sanctions over their work for the ICC have been subjected to travel bans, have had their bank accounts closed or frozen, and access to digital services denied. Because of the dominance of US financial and technology institutions, the sanctions have trickled down and affected their ability to access services in other countries as well. But the sanctions also affected rights groups not directly targeted – including the four plaintiffs – by hindering their ability to represent victims before the court, make legal and policy submissions to it, or collaborate with the sanctioned Palestinian groups on litigation, advocacy campaigns, research and humanitarian aid efforts. “Because of the sanctions regime and the threat of severe criminal and civil penalties ... if I continued my work as a lawyer as before, I would have been or could be prosecuted or fined,” Gallagher said in a press conference held by the groups on Tuesday. “I have therefore ceased actively practicing before the ICC. [...] The government cannot dictate which clients lawyers can represent, which defendants are off limits from accountability, and what venue for justice and accountability are permissible. Shawan Jabarin, the director of the human rights group Al Haq, one of the Palestinian organizations targeted by the Trump administration over its work with the ICC, told the Guardian in an interview last year that the sanctions had left the group unable to access its bank accounts or process donations, leaving about 45 people without pay. But Jabarin also said the impact of the sanctions had extended beyond logistical matters and created a climate of fear by which longtime allies had cut communications with the group to avoid running afoul of the sanctions regime, with potential punishments of up to 20 years in prison and exorbitant fines. “Most of them – if not all – they stopped working with us or engaging with us formally and openly,” Jabarin said at the time of several US groups with which Al Haq had collaborated in the past. He had called on those partners at the time to “fight back with all means”. Tuesday’s lawsuit follows one filed last month by Democracy in the Arab World Now (Dawn), a Washington-based advocacy group focused on US foreign policy in the Middle East, and the New York-based Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide, as well as legal challenges brought by some of the sanctioned individuals themselves, including Albanese’s family and three sitting ICC judges . James Goldston, executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, a program of Open Society Foundations, which the Trump administration also explicitly threatened last year, called the sanctions “an assault on the rule of law, independent judges and prosecutors, and civil society in the United States and around the world”. “Independent courts can function only when judges, prosecutors and rights advocates are free to do their work without fear of political retaliation. We believe that no one is above the law,” he said in the press conference on Tuesday. “The executive order shields the perpetrators of war crimes from scrutiny while punishing those who pursue accountability. Justice must be fair and impartial, not only directed at America’s adversaries.” Explore more on these topics Trump administration International criminal court US politics Law (US) Palestine Israel Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.politico.eu/article/france-2.text: PARIS — Brussels’ nightmare scenario for France’s 2027 presidential election is edging closer to reality. A poll published Monday showed far-left France Unbowed leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon scoring well enough in multiple scenarios to defeat the panoply of more centrist candidates and qualify for the runoff where he’d face far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen — raising the specter of a battle of extremes in the April contest. France’s presidential election sees the top two candidates advance to a second round if no one scores more than 50 percent of the vote. The survey, conducted by Toluna Harris Interactive for broadcasters M6 and RTL , found Le Pen with a commanding lead of at least 16 points ahead of her nearest competitor in every scenario tested. Advertisement Advertisement The National Rally leader has long been the favorite to win, and Mélenchon’s rise raises the risk of a runoff between two candidates who hold deeply skeptical views of the EU and NATO. In one scenario tested, which includes three candidates from the political center, the France Unbowed leader would receive 16 percent of the vote ahead of former prime ministers Édouard Philippe on 14 percent, and Gabriel Attal on 8 percent. Le Pen came in well ahead of all of them with 35 percent. Without Attal in the contest, the poll found Mélenchon and Philippe would be tied for second place at 17 percent each. Moderates have for weeks voiced concern that the field is too crowded and risks ceding the election to the political extremes. “I’ve been warning for months of the likelihood of a face-off between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon,” said government spokesperson Maud Bregeon, who is supporting Philippe’s candidacy. “The likelihood of this risk has increased, unsurprisingly.”

https://yalibnan.com/2026/09/05/hans-tho.text: Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, the ideologist behind the AFD’s plans in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany: Analysis Sep 5, 2026 Share: Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party and also member of Saxony-Anhalt’s regional parliament, in Magdeburg, eastern Germany on July 11, 2026. © Jens Schluter, AFP The far-right German political party Alternative for Germany could win a historical victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt in key elections this Sunday. The party’s agenda is more radical than ever and inspired by the proposals of an influential ideologist in the region: Hans-Thomas Tillschneider. Germany is bracing itself for a political earthquake . The Alternative for Germany (AFD) party could potentially become the first far-right party to form a state government since World War II . In the state of Saxony-Anhalt, in what was formerly East Germany, the party is polling above 40% ahead of key regional elections . Germany’s AFD party eyes outright win in regional election ‘Clearly the AFD’s most extreme program’ The region – the cradle for German Protestantism, is home to about 2.2 million people and the population will likely have to adapt to the smiling face of Ulrich Siegmund. The AFD’s top candidate is a star on social media and a specialist of punchlines. He presents himself as a “normal citizen” which all Germans can relate to. The “popstar” of the AFD – as the German press calls him – hopes to become the party’s first ever state premier. To reach his objective, Siegmund is banking on the buzz he creates on TikTok, Instagram and other platforms more than on his party’s agenda. ‘Germany is going to see tough times so it’s very important to get the economy back on track’ That task has been left up to another local politician. Hans-Thomas Tillschneider has often been described as the mastermind of the AFD in Saxony-Anhalt. The ideas of the 48-year-old politician have been the principal sources of inspiration for what is “probably the most openly extreme platform the AFD ever presented during an election” according to German media , said Jan Niklas Reiche, a political scientist and specialist of the far-right at the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg in Saxony-Anhalt. “It’s a conservative-reactionary program that proposes rolling back on 20 to 30 years of social progress, especially in recognition of the LGBTQ+ community and women’s rights. It advocates a strongly anti-immigration stance and denies the urgency of acting on global warming,” said Sven Leunig, a political scientist at the University of Jena, who studied the AFD’s agenda for the upcoming regional elections . If the far-right party wins the election on Sunday, Tillschneider’s ideas will largely shape the general political direction of Saxony-Anhalt, especially if the AFD – as some polls suggest – will govern alone. From Timisoara to Moscow, via Damas cus And Tillschneider is rarely short of ideas. “If Ulrich Siegmund is the presentable candidate who sells the party’s agenda to the public, Hans-Thomas Tillshneider is more of the mastermind of this campaign,” said Anna-Sophie Heinze, a political scientist and specialist on the far-right at the University of Lüneburg (Lower Saxony). “He considers himself as the AFD’s intellectual avant-garde and sees himself as one of the masterminds of the party in Saxony-Anhalt,” said Reiche. Tillshneider has a lengthy CV that reflects the path of a world citizen more than one of a German nationalist. The politician was born in 1978 in Timisoara, Romania , to ethnic Germans. During his university years, he became profoundly interested in Islam . Tillshneider went on to pursue studies in Islam and philosophy in Fribourg and Leipzig before travelling to the Syrian capital of Damascus. Upon his return to Germany, he completed his studies with a thesis on an 18 th century Muslim jurist. His scholarly past has led the German media to call him “Dr. Extreme right”, as website, The Pioneer underlined in a recent portrait of the politician . Yet the German public have become familiar with him in another context. Shortly after the beginning of Russia ’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Tillschneider was among the handful of AFD members who travelled to Moscow to demonstrate their solidarity with Russian President Vladimir Putin . The lawmaker even sought to visit the occupied Donbas, but his party’s leadership finally discouraged him from going. Today, Tillschneider fully embraces his pro-Russian position. In 2024, he visited the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad, situated between Poland and Lithuania . Along with other AFD members, they brandished Russian flags in support of Moscow. “Dr. Extreme right” thus became “Moscow’s warrior saint” in Germany, wrote The Pioneer. Several days ago, a journalist from the magazine Bild discovered a Russian army mug in Tillschneider’s home. A video in which the deputy tried to downplay the significance of the find has made the rounds on social media. The pro-Russian tendancy is clearly visible in the AFD’s agenda in Saxony-Anhalt. The document “calls for: an end to sanctions against Russia, Ukrainian refugees to be treated like other refugees and more Russian to be taught in schools”, said Leunig. Above anything, Tillschneider aims to lead a “culture” battle during the elections in Saxony-Anhalt. “If the AFD wins, he will inherit the expansive Ministry of Education (which oversees higher education, research and cultural affairs in Saxony-Anhalt),” said Reiche. Culture wars In its agenda, the far-right party in Saxony-Anhalt chose culture as its third priority, behind “family and children” and “immigration and remigration”. No other party has placed such a strong accent on culture; it is even a local particularity of the AFD. “The programme for Berlin mentions it on page 104 out of 114 pages. In the neighbouring state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the AFD mentions it on page 92 out of 93,” wrote daily newspaper, Süddeutsche Zeitung. Tillschneider has promised to stop “public funding promoting anti-German art” – without ever defining what kind of art falls into this category. Bauhaus, the emblematic German architectural movement which began in 1919, has also fallen into the AFD’s crosshairs. The party’s focus on the movement may seem surprising in the context of a 2026 election. Tillschneider has justified their concern, saying that Bauhaus represents “a modernity which is losing its way” – something which “takes up the vocabulary used by the Nazis to criticize the movement”, said Reiche. The Third Reich banned the artistic movement in the 1930s, calling it “degenerate art”. The AFD’s ideologist has also planned further nods to those who might harbor nostalgia for that dark period of German history. This is particularly the case in the domain of education, where he “wants more Bismarck and less Hitler”, said Reiche. Culture is often a signature issue of the far-right. “The extreme right underlines these issues – whether it’s gender or sociocultural issues related to immigration – than on the economy. Culture is often an issue that allows the far-right to garner support,” said Heinze. According to the expert, the culture war is important because it allows the AFD “to present German identity as very homogeneous”. And Tillschneider defends the idea that “German identity” should be restored through a “patriotic political culture”. The other advantage of culture as a political flashpoint is that it “allows regional action through concrete measures”, said Heinze. In contrast, immigration falls under the responsibility of the federal government. Yet for the experts interviewed, Tillschneider’s agenda is national in scope. In the case of an AFD victory on Sunday, “the state of Saxony-Anhalt will become a laboratory for the recommended measures and for the continuation of normalising” extremist discourse, said Reiche. And if the AFD in Saxony-Anhalt manages to achieve a major election victory for the German far-right, its success will be largely in part to the combination of Siegmund’s winning smile and Tillschneider’s blatant radicality. Photograph: Juan Barbosa/Reuters View image in fullscreen Demonstrators fill a Madrid city square during a housing protest on Saturday. Photograph: Juan Barbosa/Reuters Spain ‘This can’t go on’: tens of thousands protest against housing crisis in Spain Demonstrators take to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities ⁠after ​new legislation fails to pass Staff and agencies Sat 3 Oct 2026 10.19 EDT Last modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 10.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities as they step up demands for action to tackle ⁠a mounting housing crisis ⁠after ​government measures were struck down by the opposition. Demonstrators on Saturday waved posters calling for a general strike ⁠after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in ⁠Madrid, and other housing issues, were rejected in parliament on ​Friday. Authorities said 70,000 people were protesting. Organisers put the figure at 500,000. “It’s a shame,” Nando ‌de Anguulo, 26, ‌who joined the protest in Madrid, told Reuters. “It only proves that it ‌is us the people who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, may call a snap election for November after the ‌legislation failed to pass, Spanish media reported on Friday, and would be watching the strength of Saturday’s ​protests before making a decision. View image in fullscreen Thousands of demonstrators took to the streets of Madrid. Photograph: Alejandro Martinez Velez/Reuters The demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life into Sánchez’s beleaguered government and shifting attention away from the lingering impact of recent events in Ceuta . Protests on Saturday were peaceful in 50 Spanish cities. In the south-eastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police who fired rubber bullets and teargas ⁠to break up the protests. About 30 people managed to get inside ​the City ​of Arts and Sciences, a ​landmark cultural building in the city, before they were ​ousted by ‌police. One protester in Madrid, Marcos Sainz, a librarian aged 26, said he used to rent a two-bedroom apartment with friends for a monthly rent of 900 euros ($1,000) but that a one-bedroom flat often now cost 1,000 euros – or half the median monthly salary in the capital. He told AFP he would protest rental spikes “until someone dares to regulate it all as (otherwise) we’ll all have to leave Madrid and that would be a shame as I am from Madrid”. Javier, 31, a solar panel installer, said: “We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project.” He added: “I spend half of my salary on a tiny room”. “What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time, an energy that is showing that eight days of people power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government,” Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants’ Union organising the protest, said in a statement. “Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” she said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Protesters clash with police during the demonstration in Valencia. Photograph: Kai Forsterling/EPA On Friday, Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room. Despite the anger of the protesters outside parliament, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees. The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building ​more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo. View image in fullscreen A demonstrator holds up a sign reading ‘Right to a Roof’ on Plaza de Espana in Madrid. Photograph: Javier Soriano/AFP/Getty Images News of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted. The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was evicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years . The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment. Reuters and AFP contributed to this report. https://www.dw.com/en/german-spy-scandal.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NuOO The arrest of August Hanning, former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), is threatening to cause a major rupture in Germany's intelligence relationships Image: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement The arrests of August Hanning , former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) , and his former chief-of-staff, Manfred D.*, are threatening to cause a major rupture in Germany's intelligence relationships, according to analysts, as the full scale of the scandal begins to be understood abroad. Manfred D. is accused of selling around 2,000 highly classified documents to Hanning over a period of 12 years, long after the latter stepped down from the BND in 2005 following seven years as its chief. Manfred D. continued to serve all of Hanning's successors, including the current BND chief Martin Jäger, before retiring in March this year. On one occasion, the state prosecutor said, Hanning "used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D. to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service." DW's Michaela Küfner looks at Germany's espionage scandal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video According to Florian Flade, a reporter for public broadcaster ARD, most of these documents were weekly intelligence briefings the BND delivered to the German government, including the latest findings from partner intelligence agencies in other countries. "This is very, very sensitive because it involves partner agencies in other countries," Flade told DW's Berlin Briefing podcast . "And we heard this also involves information about the Iranian nuclear program, the Russian military, also the Ukraine war." Broken trust, broken credibility Some pundits now say that the biggest concern is what conclusions the intelligence agencies of allied countries will draw from this affair. In the past, the Central Intelligence Agency in the US is known to have shared information on radical Islamists in Germany, which possibly helped to prevent terrorist attacks in the country. If it now emerges that information was leaving the BND via Hanning, that relationship could be undermined, particularly if it was also eventually ending up in the hands of the intelligence agencies of Russia and China — though there is no suggestion of that as yet. "There's huge damage being done not only to the outer appearance and image of the BND," said Flade. "There's a damage assessment now happening within the BND. Also, they're talking to partners about this because they want to know if their information was given to other countries." That could also potentially have consequences for Germany's national security in the growing confrontation with Russia. The BND, which is currently subject to more legal restrictions than other intelligence agencies around the world, considers its relationship with its US counterpart as vital. "There might be a change in the amount of information that is coming from the US and others," Flade added. Ultimately, he pointed out, it might be difficult for the BND to know what they're not being told. Security loopholes in Germany's parliament spark concern To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Only a day before the scandal broke, current BND President Martin Jäger reiterated his concern that Germany could slide into a military conflict with Russia, telling a parliamentary hearing that the Kremlin was already waging a "shadow war" and that further military rearmament was "unfortunately necessary" — though he did say that there was currently no indication of active preparations from Russia. Flade said that, behind the scenes, Jäger is furious about the leak of information from Manfred D. and called a meeting on Tuesday of all BND officials to underline how serious the consequences of sharing information could be. New internal security measures are also being put in place. The new case could not have come at a worse time for Jäger or the BND. For one thing, new laws are currently being prepared to expand the agency's powers, partly to improve the BND's standing among its foreign partners. For another thing, another BND agent, Carsten L. and a businessman named Arthur E., are currently on trial in Berlin on treason charges for passing on classified documents to the Russian secret service in 2022. Florian Flade is an espionage expert and guest in DW's Berlin Briefing podcast this week Image: DW New rules for old officials? The case has also raised questions about what former intelligence officials should and shouldn't be allowed to do once they leave office. After leaving the BND, Hanning founded his own security consultancy business, where he apparently used his contacts and knowledge to advise his clients. This is legal and tolerated, but many think it shouldn't be. Timo Lange of the NGO LobbyControl said that the Hanning case shows why former intelligence officials must be prevented from working as security consultants in any capacity for the rest of their lives. "It is fundamentally problematic when high-ranking officials from the intelligence or military sectors, after leaving government service, act as consultants for various — and in some cases unknown — clients from abroad," Lange said in a statement. "This is an obvious gateway for illegitimate foreign influence and jeopardizes the security interests of Germany and the European Union." But as Flade pointed out, Hanning's career path is not exactly unusual. "These people are trying to just make some money with what they can do best, which is networking and then selling the security assessments that they do," he said. "And yeah, working for companies or even for other countries as a consultant." Edited by Rina Goldenberg Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases. (Image: AFP) NATO commander says alliance is ready to fight if attacked. Rising concerns over suspected Russian sabotage in Europe. NATO strategy focuses on blocking, blunting, and breaking. Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Register for FREE Webinar Register for FREE NATO’s top military commander, General Alexus G Grynkewich, said on Monday the alliance was “ready to fight tonight” if attacked, as European governments grapple with suspected Russian sabotage and questions over the reliability of US security guarantees. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe said a conflict with Russia was neither imminent nor inevitable. He outlined a strategy designed to stop an attack on allied territory, prevent enemy forces from advancing and, if necessary, dismantle the military systems supporting an offensive. Although Grynkewich did not explicitly name Russia in his remarks, his warning came amid heightened tensions between European governments and Moscow. Russia has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage and other covert operations, Reuters reported. Russian sabotage concerns raise tensions in Europe Recent incidents have heightened European concerns over suspected Russian sabotage and other covert operations. Related Stories Who is Beatrice Keul? Former Miss Switzerland contestant accuses Trump of rape in 1993. Here's what ... 'Canada Won’t Sign Trump’s August Offer’: Mark Carney’s Blunt Take On U.S. Trade Deal Trump Slams Obama As 'LOUSY President' In Reply To Cheesecake Factory Remark Germany reported an alleged plot targeting a Ukrainian aircraft at Leipzig airport, while Estonia blamed Russia for an arson attack on a defence company. British officials have also said they foiled a Russian plot targeting a drone facility near London. The incidents have added to concerns about covert activity across Europe, although the allegations and attribution differ from case to case. Polish officials have cited more than 210 acts of sabotage attributed to Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, The Associated Press reported. The figure reflects incidents attributed to Moscow by officials, rather than independently established Russian responsibility for every case. Separately, Denmark’s defence intelligence service has warned of a “low but growing risk” of a limited Russian military attack against NATO countries bordering Russia. It has also warned that Moscow could use covert operations to weaken the alliance’s unity. However, the assessment noted that an outright attack on NATO would be difficult while Russia remains engaged in its war against Ukraine, according to AP. NATO’s US commitment under scrutiny European concerns over Russian activity have coincided with questions about the reliability of US security guarantees under President Donald Trump , who has pressed NATO allies to take greater responsibility for their own defence. During his election campaign, Trump said he would allow Russia to “do whatever the hell they want” with NATO allies that failed to meet his demands on defence spending. The remarks raised concerns in Europe about Washington’s commitment to NATO’s collective defence principle, under which an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all. Grynkewich sought to reassure European allies about Washington’s commitment, pointing to the presence of American military personnel along NATO’s eastern flank. “No one should question the commitment of the United States to this alliance,” he said, adding that he was in Europe as an American officer sent by Trump. Poland hosts around 10,000 US troops and borders Ukraine, Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave, making it strategically important to NATO’s eastern defences. Questions about US support have also extended to military assistance for Ukraine. The Financial Times has reported that European officials said Washington threatened to halt a programme supplying US weapons to Ukraine and cut intelligence sharing to pressure Kyiv to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. The reported threat raised concerns about transatlantic security cooperation, but does not establish that either weapons supplies or intelligence sharing was subsequently suspended. Assistance to Ukraine is distinct from the US commitment to defend NATO members under the alliance’s collective defence arrangements. ‘Block, blunt, break’: NATO’s strategy against Russia Grynkewich outlined what he called NATO’s “theory of victory”, built around three stages: blocking an initial attack, blunting the advance of enemy forces and, if necessary, breaking the military system supporting the offensive. “We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational war-fighting system arrayed against us,” he said. The approach would target not only forces directly involved in an assault but also the wider systems supporting, sustaining and controlling them. Grynkewich said NATO would act if an adversary continued an attack or committed reserves, with the objective of breaking the warfighting system engaged against the alliance. He said NATO’s goal would be to prevent an adversary from seizing and holding allied territory, rather than capturing Russian land. He did not specify a particular attack scenario, location or composition of enemy forces. Grynkewich also highlighted the need to apply lessons from the wars in Ukraine and West Asia, where drones and other relatively inexpensive systems have been deployed alongside precision weapons. He called for “affordable mass” — combining advanced capabilities with scalable systems such as drones, autonomous technologies and electronic warfare — to strengthen NATO’s ability to respond to a potential attack.
